questions: Can the subgraph be any subset of vertices and edges of T, or must it be an induced subgraph (i.e., must include all edges of T between the chosen vertices)?
When counting the number of vertices in the alkane subgraph, should isolated vertices (degree 0) be allowed, or must every selected vertex have degree exactly 1 or 4 within the subgraph?
Is a single edge (two vertices of degree 1) considered a valid alkane if there is no vertex of degree 4, or must the subgraph contain at least one degree‑4 vertex to be accepted?

If multiple subgraphs satisfy the conditions with the same maximum number of vertices, does the output need to follow any particular tie‑breaking rule (e.g., smallest lexicographic set of vertices) or is any such maximum size acceptable?

Are vertices of degree 4 in the subgraph required to have exactly four incident edges within the subgraph, or can they have more incident edges in the original tree as long as only four of them are selected?
Must the subgraph itself be connected, or is a disconnected collection of tree components allowed as long as each component is a tree with the degree constraints?
Are self‑loops or multiple edges possible in the input, and if so, how should they be treated when forming the subgraph?
Should the answer be printed as a single integer (the maximum number of vertices) or is additional output (e.g., the list of vertices) ever required?
answers: Not specified beyond what's given; assume the subgraph must be induced, i.e. contain all edges of T between the selected vertices.
Not specified beyond what's given; every selected vertex must have degree exactly 1 or 4 within the subgraph, so isolated vertices are not allowed.
No, the alkane definition explicitly requires at least one vertex of degree 4; a subgraph with only degree-1 vertices does not qualify.
Not specified beyond what's given; any maximum-size subgraph is acceptable, no tie-breaking rule is required.
Not specified beyond what's given; a degree-4 vertex's four incident edges are counted within the subgraph itself, regardless of its degree in the original tree.
Not specified beyond what's given; assume the subgraph must remain a single connected tree.
Not applicable; the input is a tree, which by definition has no self-loops or multiple edges.
Only the number of vertices in the largest alkane subgraph should be printed, not the vertices themselves.
inline_prompts: You are given an undirected tree T with N vertices, numbered 1, 2, \ldots, N. The i-th edge is an undirected edge connecting vertices A_i and B_i. A graph is defined to be an alkane if and only if it satisfies the following conditions: - The graph is an undirected tree. - Every vertex has degree 1 or 4, and there is at least one vertex of degree 4. Not specified beyond what's given; assume the subgraph must be induced, i.e. contain all edges of T between the selected vertices. Determine whether there exists a subgraph of T that is an alkane, and if so, find the maximum number of vertices in such a subgraph. Input The input is given from Standard Input in the following format: N A_1 B_1 A_2 B_2 \vdots A_{N - 1} B_{N - 1} Output If there exists a subgraph of T that is an alkane, print the answer. Otherwise, print -1. Constraints - 1 \leq N \leq 2 \times 10^5 - 1 \leq A_i, B_i \leq N - The given graph is an undirected tree. - All input values are integers.
